{"claims": [
{"id": "c1", "text": "The paper argues that a node's importance and its functional role are codependent. Circuit discovery and functional interpretation should therefore be solved jointly rather than as two sequential stages. Doing so faces two challenges: role labels in prior work are node- and task-specific, and they are assigned subjectively.", "sections": ["s0", "s1", "s5"], "depends_on": []},
{"id": "c2", "text": "Node behavior is abstracted into two task-agnostic computational roles: functional nodes, which transform their inputs, and passthrough nodes, which relocate information with little change. The dichotomy describes how a node processes information, not what content it processes. The specific roles in the IOI and Acronym circuits map consistently onto it.", "sections": ["s1", "s2"], "depends_on": ["c1"]},
{"id": "c3", "text": "Each node carries three learnable coefficients (unimportant, passthrough, functional) that should sum to one. A node is a circuit candidate if c_p + c_f > c_u. The discovery stage minimizes an α-weighted mix of KL divergence to the full model and cross-entropy on the true answer. Hard argmax assignments are used only at evaluation.", "sections": ["s3"], "depends_on": ["c1", "c2"]},
{"id": "c4", "text": "Roles are assigned with a quantitative FI metric: the normalized Frobenius change in off-diagonal token-wise cosine similarity between a node's input and its output. The classification loss rewards c_f in proportion to FI and rewards c_p in inverse proportion to FI.", "sections": ["s3"], "depends_on": ["c2", "c3"]},
{"id": "c5", "text": "Training uses a regularizer with confidence, validity and sparsity terms. A warmup phase runs the discovery objective alone. After warmup, training alternates between one discovery step and k classification steps, so importance and role influence each other in both directions.", "sections": ["s3", "s4"], "depends_on": ["c3", "c4"]},
{"id": "c6", "text": "Evaluation ablates the discovered circuit, so a more negative accuracy drop means better circuit discovery. S³martCirc achieves the largest accuracy drop and logit difference across GPT-2, Llama and Qwen on both tasks. It does not always find the smallest circuit, and it runs much faster than patching methods.", "sections": ["s4", "s7"], "depends_on": ["c3", "c5"]},
{"id": "c7", "text": "S³martCirc recovers a larger share of the human-verified IOI circuit than most baselines; only Activation Patching is comparable. It recovers 4 of the 8 Acronym circuit nodes, with role labels matching the Figure 1 mapping. Disagreements on heads 8.11 and 10.10 are attributed to those heads being multi-functional.", "sections": ["s4", "s8"], "depends_on": ["c2", "c4", "c6"]},
{"id": "c8", "text": "Parameter and ablation studies show three things. First, α=0.75 is best for GPT-2 IOI, and dropping the cross-entropy term (α=1) degrades performance sharply. Second, performance improves with k up to about 6. Third, removing warmup or replacing alternation with discovery-first or interpretation-first ordering hurts; discovery-first is worst.", "sections": ["s4"], "depends_on": ["c3", "c5"]}
],
"items": [
{"id": "q1", "claim": "c1", "kind": "claim", "form": "change-condition", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s1", "s2"], "question": "Suppose S³martCirc's two general roles were replaced by the fine-grained IOI role labels from Wang et al. (e.g., S-inhibition head, name mover head). Which of the paper's two stated challenges would this reintroduce, and why would the same objective then not carry over to the Acronym task?", "answer": "It would reintroduce the first challenge, node-specific interpretations. Those labels are tied to particular nodes in the IOI task and give no shared abstraction. The Acronym circuit has different roles, such as letter movers and bridge heads, so the IOI labels would not apply to it.", "rubric": ["Identifies the node-specific (task-bound) interpretation challenge", "Explains that IOI-specific labels do not exist or apply in the Acronym circuit, so there is no general abstraction shared across tasks"]},
{"id": "q2", "claim": "c1", "kind": "claim", "form": "connect-sections", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s1", "s3"], "question": "The paper claims role information should influence which nodes are deemed important, not just the reverse. Given how S³martCirc decides whether a node is a candidate, explain concretely how a classification-stage update can change a node's importance status.", "answer": "Importance is decided by whether c_p + c_f exceeds c_u. The classification loss directly changes c_p and c_f, so a classification update can raise or lower that sum relative to c_u. This can move a node into or out of the candidate set used by the next discovery step.", "rubric": ["States that the candidate criterion compares c_p + c_f against c_u", "Notes that the classification stage updates c_p and c_f, which therefore can flip importance status across alternating steps"]},
{"id": "q3", "claim": "c1", "kind": "claim", "form": "connect-sections", "level": "textbase", "sections": ["s1", "s3"], "question": "Which specific component of S³martCirc is the paper's answer to its second challenge (subjective functional roles)? What measurable quantity does that component compute, which lets roles enter an optimization objective?", "answer": "The FI metric addresses the second challenge. It measures how much the pairwise token-wise similarity structure changes between a node's input and its output activations. Because this is a numeric quantity computed from activations, it can be placed directly in the classification loss instead of relying on human judgment.", "rubric": ["Names the FI (functional interpretation) metric", "Says FI measures the change in token-wise similarity between a node's input and output", "Notes that being numeric and computed from activations lets it be used in the loss rather than requiring human judgment"]},
{"id": "q4", "claim": "c2", "kind": "claim", "form": "apply-new-case", "level": "textbase", "sections": ["s2"], "question": "Under the paper's mapping from node-specific roles to its two general roles, how would an Acronym-circuit bridge head and an IOI name mover head each be classified, and why?", "answer": "The bridge head is passthrough because it propagates letter information downstream. The name mover head is functional because it transforms information to selectively amplify specific names in the output logits.", "rubric": ["Bridge head is labeled passthrough", "Name mover head is labeled functional", "Justification: bridge heads propagate information, while name movers transform it to amplify specific outputs"]},
{"id": "q5", "claim": "c2", "kind": "claim", "form": "apply-new-case", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s2"], "question": "Previous token heads appear in both circuits the paper examines. Under the paper's dichotomy, do they get the same general label in both tasks? What does this illustrate about the dichotomy?", "answer": "Yes, they are passthrough in both circuits, because they write or propagate previous-token information with little transformation. This holds even though the content differs (names versus letters). It illustrates that the dichotomy classifies how a node operates on information rather than what information it carries, which is what lets the roles generalize across tasks.", "rubric": ["States that previous token heads are passthrough in both tasks", "Explains that the dichotomy depends on how a node processes information rather than its content, enabling cross-task generalization"]},
{"id": "q6", "claim": "c2", "kind": "claim", "form": "spot-wrong-version", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s2", "s3"], "question": "A reader argues that IOI S-inhibition heads must be functional nodes in the paper's dichotomy because they strongly affect the model's final answer. Why is this reasoning inconsistent with how the paper defines and assigns roles?", "answer": "Affecting the answer bears on a node's importance, which the paper models with a separate coefficient. The role depends only on whether the node transforms or merely relocates information. The paper classifies S-inhibition heads as passthrough because they route subject information downstream.", "rubric": ["States that S-inhibition heads are passthrough in the paper", "Explains that influence on the answer reflects importance (c_u versus c_p + c_f), whereas the role reflects transforming versus relocating information"]},
{"id": "q7", "claim": "c3", "kind": "claim", "form": "apply-new-case", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s3"], "question": "A node ends training with coefficients c_u = 0.4, c_p = 0.35, c_f = 0.25. Is it a candidate circuit node under S³martCirc's selection rule? What label would the paper's evaluation-time hard assignment (Eq. 1) give it?", "answer": "It is a candidate during training, because c_p + c_f = 0.6 > 0.4. However, Eq. 1 takes the argmax over the three individual coefficients, and c_u = 0.4 is the largest, so the hard assignment labels it unimportant. The two rules therefore disagree for this node.", "rubric": ["Computes c_p + c_f = 0.6 > 0.4, so the node is a candidate", "Notes that the argmax over individual coefficients picks c_u, giving the label unimportant (the rules disagree)"]},
{"id": "q8", "claim": "c3", "kind": "claim", "form": "change-condition", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s3"], "question": "If S³martCirc's discovery objective (Eq. 2) were run with α = 0, what would the objective reduce to? Which of its two stated goals would no longer be enforced?", "answer": "With α = 0 the KL term vanishes, leaving only the cross-entropy on the ground-truth token. The circuit would still be pushed to give correct answers, but it would no longer be pushed to faithfully reproduce the full model's output distribution.", "rubric": ["States that the objective reduces to cross-entropy on the ground-truth answer only", "Identifies faithfulness to the original model's distribution (the KL term) as no longer enforced"]},
{"id": "q9", "claim": "c6", "kind": "claim", "form": "connect-sections", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s3", "s4"], "question": "In the paper's evaluation, why does a better discovered circuit produce a more negative accuracy drop rather than a smaller one? Answer using how P_circ is constructed and the paper's rationale for what makes a node important.", "answer": "At evaluation, P_circ masks the circuit nodes themselves. The paper defines important nodes as those whose removal substantially degrades task performance. So if the method has found the truly critical nodes, removing them should cause a large accuracy drop, which is recorded as a large negative value.", "rubric": ["Notes that P_circ masks or removes the circuit nodes at evaluation", "Connects this to the paper's premise that removing truly important nodes should substantially degrade performance, so a larger drop means a better circuit"]},
{"id": "q10", "claim": "c4", "kind": "claim", "form": "apply-new-case", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s3"], "question": "Consider a node whose output preserves every off-diagonal pairwise token similarity of its input exactly. What FI value does the paper's metric give it? Which role does the paper's classification loss push it toward, and why?", "answer": "FI is 0, because Sim(X) − Sim(Y) is the zero matrix. In L_class the passthrough term is −c_p/FI, which becomes extremely negative as FI approaches zero, while the functional reward −c_f·FI vanishes. The loss is therefore minimized by putting weight on c_p, so the node is pushed toward passthrough.", "rubric": ["States FI = 0 (or near zero)", "Concludes the node is pushed toward passthrough", "Reason: the −c_p/FI term dominates as FI approaches 0, while the c_f·FI reward vanishes"]},
{"id": "q11", "claim": "c4", "kind": "claim", "form": "connect-sections", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s2", "s3"], "question": "A node's input has the model's hidden dimension, while its output has the node's own output dimension; for a feedforward neuron this is 1. Why can the paper's FI metric still compare input and output directly?", "answer": "FI does not compare the activations themselves. It compares their token-by-token similarity matrices, and the Sim operator turns any T×d matrix into a T×T matrix of pairwise token similarities. Input and output similarity matrices therefore always have the same shape and can be subtracted, whatever their feature dimensions.", "rubric": ["States that the Sim operator maps both input and output to T×T token-similarity matrices", "Concludes that the feature-dimension mismatch is irrelevant because only the T×T matrices are compared"]},
{"id": "q12", "claim": "c4", "kind": "claim", "form": "spot-wrong-version", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s3"], "question": "Suppose the paper's classification loss were altered so the passthrough term also rewarded FI: each node's term becomes −c_f·FI − c_p·FI. Why would this break the classification the paper intends?", "answer": "The node's term would become −(c_f + c_p)·FI, so the loss could no longer tell the two roles apart. Low-FI nodes would no longer be steered toward passthrough. The original inverse term −c_p/FI is what makes passthrough preferred when FI is small and functional preferred when FI is large.", "rubric": ["Notes the altered loss depends only on c_f + c_p, so it cannot distinguish the roles", "Explains that the inverse dependence of the c_p term on FI is what assigns low-FI (similarity-preserving) nodes to passthrough"]},
{"id": "q13", "claim": "c5", "kind": "claim", "form": "apply-new-case", "level": "textbase", "sections": ["s3"], "question": "Using the confidence term of the paper's regularizer (Eq. 5), what penalty does a single coefficient of 0.5 incur compared with a coefficient of 1.0? What training behavior does this difference encourage?", "answer": "A value of 0.5 incurs ½·|0.5·0.5| = 0.125, while 1.0 incurs ½·|1·0| = 0. The term therefore pushes coefficients toward binary values (0 or 1), giving confident assignments.", "rubric": ["Computes 0.125 for 0.5 and 0 for 1.0", "Concludes the term encourages coefficients to become binary or confident"]},
{"id": "q14", "claim": "c5", "kind": "claim", "form": "change-condition", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s3"], "question": "If S³martCirc's three per-node coefficients were produced by a softmax over three logits instead of being free parameters, which term of its regularizer would become redundant, and why?", "answer": "The validity term would be redundant. Its only purpose is to push c_u + c_p + c_f toward 1, and a softmax output always sums to exactly one, so that term would always be zero.", "rubric": ["Identifies the validity term", "Reason: a softmax already guarantees that the three values sum to one"]},
{"id": "q15", "claim": "c5", "kind": "claim", "form": "apply-new-case", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s3", "s4"], "question": "Using the paper's definition of an iteration in its parameter analysis, how many discovery steps and how many classification steps occur in 10 post-warmup iterations with k = 6? Why does the paper not begin these alternating iterations from the very first training step?", "answer": "There would be 10 discovery steps and 60 classification steps. The paper first runs a warmup on the discovery objective alone, because assigning roles from randomly initialized coefficients is unreliable before a reasonable set of important nodes has been identified.", "rubric": ["Computes 10 discovery and 60 classification steps", "Explains that warmup is used because role assignment with random initial coefficients is unreliable"]},
{"id": "q16", "claim": "c6", "kind": "claim", "form": "apply-new-case", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s4"], "question": "Using Table 1 for the GPT-2 Acronym setting, compare the Random baseline with S³martCirc in circuit size and accuracy drop. What does this comparison show, according to the paper's reasoning about circuit size?", "answer": "Both have an average circuit size of 60.33. Random causes a 0% accuracy drop, while S³martCirc causes −97.50%. At equal size, S³martCirc's advantage must come from choosing the right nodes, not simply more nodes, which supports the paper's claim of more effective node selection.", "rubric": ["Notes the equal circuit size (about 60) with 0% versus −97.5% accuracy drop", "Concludes that the gain reflects better node selection rather than larger circuits"]},
{"id": "q17", "claim": "c6", "kind": "claim", "form": "connect-sections", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s3", "s4"], "question": "Prune. and IBCircuit, like S³martCirc, optimize continuous masks, yet they perform far worse in Table 1. What does the paper conclude from this, and which part of S³martCirc does that conclusion credit?", "answer": "The paper concludes that masking alone is not enough. Incorporating functional interpretation provides essential guidance for identifying circuit nodes, so the conclusion credits the Important Node Classification stage (the FI-based role assignment coupled into training).", "rubric": ["States that continuous masking by itself does not explain S³martCirc's advantage", "Credits the functional-interpretation / Important Node Classification stage"]},
{"id": "q18", "claim": "c6", "kind": "claim", "form": "connect-sections", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s4", "s7"], "question": "Using the paper's runtime table, roughly how many times faster is S³martCirc than Activation Patching on Qwen IOI? What feature of how Activation Patching works, as described in the baselines, explains its cost?", "answer": "About 179 times faster (187,664 s versus 1,048 s). Activation Patching ablates each node individually and re-evaluates the model, so its cost grows with the number of nodes. S³martCirc instead optimizes masks over all nodes jointly.", "rubric": ["Gives a ratio of roughly 170–180×", "Explains that Activation Patching evaluates or ablates nodes one at a time"]},
{"id": "q19", "claim": "c7", "kind": "claim", "form": "spot-wrong-version", "level": "textbase", "sections": ["s2", "s4"], "question": "Suppose S³martCirc had labeled the Acronym circuit's Letter Mover head 11.4 as a passthrough node. Under the paper's Figure 1 mapping, would this count as agreement with the human-derived circuit? Why or why not?", "answer": "No. The mapping assigns letter mover heads to the functional role, because they transform letter information to emphasize the correct output. A passthrough label would contradict it.", "rubric": ["Concludes this would be a disagreement", "Reason: letter movers map to functional because they transform information rather than relocate it"]},
{"id": "q20", "claim": "c7", "kind": "claim", "form": "change-condition", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s4"], "question": "The paper explains why S³martCirc labels heads 8.11 and 10.10 differently from each other. If prior work had instead shown that head 10.10 acts only as a Bridge head under every intervention, would the paper's explanation still justify S³martCirc's label for 10.10? Explain.", "answer": "No. The explanation relies on 10.10 being multi-functional, able to act as either a bridge or a letter mover, so S³martCirc's functional label reflects its dominant contribution. If 10.10 were purely a bridge head, the mapping would make it passthrough, and the functional label would be a genuine misclassification.", "rubric": ["Concludes the explanation would no longer hold (it would be a misclassification)", "Reason: the justification depends on the head being multi-functional, and bridge heads map to passthrough"]},
{"id": "q21", "claim": "c7", "kind": "claim", "form": "connect-sections", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s4"], "question": "Activation Patching is the only baseline whose IOI circuit recovery is comparable to S³martCirc's. Using Table 1, what distinguishes S³martCirc from Activation Patching on GPT-2 IOI in accuracy drop?", "answer": "S³martCirc reaches about −96% with a small standard deviation (about 2.9). Activation Patching reaches only about −71% with a large standard deviation (about 26). So even with similar recovery of known nodes, S³martCirc's circuits are more critical and more consistent.", "rubric": ["Cites S³martCirc at about −96% versus Activation Patching at about −71%", "Notes Activation Patching's much larger variance, or concludes that S³martCirc's circuits are more critical or consistent"]},
{"id": "q22", "claim": "c8", "kind": "claim", "form": "change-condition", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s3", "s4"], "question": "According to the paper's parameter analysis, what happens to S³martCirc on GPT-2 IOI when the discovery objective is set to α = 1.0? What does the paper infer from this about baselines?", "answer": "Performance degrades sharply, because α = 1.0 removes the cross-entropy term and leaves only the KL term. The paper infers that baselines relying mainly on output-distribution differences miss critical components, since some nodes contribute to correct behavior without causing large changes in the logits.", "rubric": ["States that performance degrades sharply because the cross-entropy term is removed", "Explains the inference: methods relying only on output-distribution or logit differences miss components that support correct answers without large logit changes"]},
{"id": "q23", "claim": "c8", "kind": "claim", "form": "connect-sections", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s4"], "question": "Which of the paper's ablation variants tests whether functional information helps discovery even without alternating training? What did its result show relative to the discovery-first variant and the full method?", "answer": "S³martCirc-IF (interpretation first) tests this. It clearly outperformed S³martCirc-DF, showing that role information is a useful prior for discovery. It still underperformed the full method, showing that this prior is insufficient without alternation.", "rubric": ["Identifies the interpretation-first (IF) variant", "States it beat DF but was worse than full S³martCirc", "Interprets this: functional information helps as a prior but alternation is still needed"]},
{"id": "q24", "claim": "c8", "kind": "claim", "form": "connect-sections", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s4"], "question": "The paper explains the failure of S³martCirc-DF in terms of the candidate set handed to classification. Given that explanation, why does alternating training specifically benefit the classification stage?", "answer": "Under DF, classification receives an overly broad, noisy candidate set and cannot separate critical nodes from less relevant ones. Under alternation, classification repeatedly works on candidate sets that discovery has progressively narrowed, so its role assignments operate on more focused, less noisy sets.", "rubric": ["Notes that DF gives classification an overly broad, noisy candidate set", "Explains that alternation lets classification work on progressively more focused candidate sets"]},
{"id": "q25", "claim": "c8", "kind": "claim", "form": "apply-new-case", "level": "textbase", "sections": ["s4"], "question": "A practitioner runs S³martCirc on GPT-2 IOI with k = 2 to save time. Based on the paper's parameter analysis, what accuracy drop should they expect compared with k = 6? What happens to IOI circuit recovery?", "answer": "They should expect roughly −71% instead of about −96%, a substantially weaker circuit. Circuit recovery would also be lower, since it increased monotonically with k.", "rubric": ["Expects about −71% at k = 2 versus about −96% at k = 6", "Notes that circuit recovery would also be lower because it rises monotonically with k"]},
{"id": "q26", "claim": "c8", "kind": "integration", "form": "connect-sections", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s4", "s7"], "question": "The paper's parameter analysis found a best α for GPT-2 IOI. According to the appendix hyperparameters, which Table 1 model–task runs used a different α? What does this imply about the scope of the parameter-analysis finding?", "answer": "Acronym with GPT-2 and IOI with Llama both used α = 0.25, while the parameter analysis found α = 0.75 best for GPT-2 IOI. The best balance between KL and cross-entropy therefore varies with task and model, consistent with the paper scoping its finding to 'for the IOI task'.", "rubric": ["Identifies GPT-2 Acronym and Llama IOI (α = 0.25)", "Concludes that the optimal α is task- or model-dependent, so the α = 0.75 finding does not generalize automatically"]},
{"id": "q27", "claim": "c4", "kind": "integration", "form": "connect-sections", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s3", "s6"], "question": "The paper's conclusion admits that the same node may be labeled differently across tasks. Which property of how S³martCirc's role metric is computed makes this possible?", "answer": "FI is computed from a node's actual input and output activations on the task's prompts, through the token-similarity matrices. Different tasks supply different tokens, and so different similarity structures, so the same node can change similarity a lot on one task and little on another, yielding different roles.", "rubric": ["Notes that FI is computed from task-specific input and output activations (token similarities)", "Explains that different task inputs can give different FI values and hence different role labels for the same node"]},
{"id": "q28", "claim": "c6", "kind": "integration", "form": "connect-sections", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s4", "s7"], "question": "On Qwen Acronym, Activation Patching matches S³martCirc's accuracy drop in Table 1. Why should that baseline result be weighted less than S³martCirc's? How does the runtime appendix explain the reason?", "answer": "The Activation Patching entry is marked as coming from a single run because of the 48-hour limit, so it has no variance estimate. S³martCirc's result is averaged over three runs. The runtime table shows why: Activation Patching took roughly 169,000 seconds (about 47 hours) on Qwen Acronym, so repeated runs would not fit the time limit.", "rubric": ["Notes that the Activation Patching result is from only one run (asterisk) versus three runs for S³martCirc", "Links this to the runtime table, which shows Activation Patching takes about 169k seconds (near the 48-hour limit) on Qwen"]},
{"id": "q29", "claim": "c1", "kind": "integration", "form": "connect-sections", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s1", "s4"], "question": "The introduction cites a view that the two MI stages can be performed in reverse order. Which ablation variant implements that reversed ordering? Does its result support treating the stages as a single jointly optimized problem rather than just reordering them?", "answer": "S³martCirc-IF implements interpretation before discovery. It beat discovery-first but still underperformed full alternating S³martCirc. This supports the paper's view that reordering is not enough and the stages should be coupled bidirectionally.", "rubric": ["Identifies the IF (interpretation first) variant", "Notes it outperforms DF but underperforms the full method", "Concludes that this supports joint or alternating optimization over mere reordering"]}
]}

ANSWER Q1: FI would be 0 (minimum), since the metric measures how much the node *rewrites* token-geometry and a perfect similarity-preserving map transforms nothing. The classification loss therefore pushes it toward the passthrough role, because the passthrough coefficient is rewarded for low FI (preservation) while the functional coefficient is rewarded by high FI (transformation).

ANSWER Q2: Yes — in both IOI and Acronym the previous token heads receive the same general label, passthrough, because in both tasks they copy prior-token information without altering its similarity structure. This illustrates that the dichotomy's labels track the *type of computation* and are therefore task-general, unlike fine-grained role names that must be redefined per task.

ANSWER Q3: With an iteration defined as k discovery steps followed by k classification steps, 10 post-warmup iterations at k = 6 give 60 discovery steps and 60 classification steps. The warmup is needed because classification assigns roles using the current candidate masks; alternating from step 0 would compute FI and role gradients on essentially random masks, injecting noise into discovery and labeling a meaningless candidate set.

ANSWER Q4: They should expect essentially the same accuracy drop as with k = 6 — the parameter analysis reports the method is robust to k, with k = 2 performing within noise of k = 6. IOI circuit recovery (overlap with the known circuit) is likewise basically unchanged, indicating k controls the per-alternation step budget, not which nodes are found.

ANSWER Q5: That is the classification-first variant (S³martCirc-CF), which computes roles once and then runs discovery with role/FI information but no alternation. It outperformed the discovery-first variant — showing functional information genuinely helps discovery — but remained clearly worse than the full alternating method, showing the alternation itself contributes additional gains.

ANSWER Q6: No, it would not count as agreement. Under the Figure 1 mapping, a Letter Mover head corresponds to the functional role (it converts word identity into initial-letter identity, altering token geometry), so a passthrough label disagrees with the human-derived circuit once labels are mapped to the two general roles.

ANSWER Q7: The normalization (simplex) term that penalizes deviation of c_u + c_p + c_f from 1 would become redundant, because a softmax over three logits guarantees positive coefficients summing to 1 by construction.

ANSWER Q8: Both role coefficients would then receive identical FI-weighted reward, so the loss provides no gradient distinguishing transformation from copying. The functional/passthrough split would collapse — assignment between the two roles becomes arbitrary (decided only by the other terms), destroying exactly the distinction the classification stage exists to produce.

ANSWER Q9: Yes, it is still a candidate circuit node: the selection rule keeps a node whenever the unimportant coefficient is not dominant in aggregate, i.e., c_p + c_f = 0.6 > c_u = 0.4. However, the evaluation-time hard assignment (Eq. 1) takes the argmax, so it would be labeled "unimportant" — illustrating the difference between the soft selection rule and the hard role assignment.

ANSWER Q10: The paper concludes that continuous mask optimization by itself is not the source of S³martCirc's advantage, since Prune. and IBCircuit share that machinery yet perform far worse. It credits the role-aware component — functional-information-guided classification combined with alternating training — for the improvement.

ANSWER Q11: In S³martCirc-DF, classification receives a fixed candidate set produced by a one-shot discovery phase, which is noisy and mis-inclusive, so classification wastes effort labeling spurious candidates and cannot recover missing ones. Alternating training continually refreshes the candidate set, so classification always operates on the current best circuit estimate, and its FI-based gradients in turn prune or reinstate candidates — the two stages correct each other's errors.

ANSWER Q12: The classification-first (S³martCirc-CF) variant implements the reversed ordering. Its underperformance relative to full S³martCirc indicates that merely reordering the stages is insufficient, supporting the paper's claim that discovery and classification should be treated as one jointly (alternatingly) optimized problem.

ANSWER Q13: A node is a candidate when its unimportant coefficient is not dominant (c_p + c_f > c_u). A classification-stage update that finds high FI raises c_f (or, for a copying node, c_p), and because the coefficients are constrained to sum to one, c_u is driven down — e.g., a node moving from (0.6, 0.4, 0.0) to (0.4, 0.6, 0.0) flips from excluded to included in P_circ, so the role update literally changes its importance status.

ANSWER Q14: The paper defines roles by representational transformation (FI) and assigns them via learned coefficients optimized with the FI-based classification loss — not by causal influence on the output. A passthrough node can be causally decisive (e.g., a name mover determines the answer while merely copying), so "strongly affects the answer ⇒ functional" conflates importance with role, exactly the confusion the dichotomy separates.

ANSWER Q15: At α = 1.0 the minimality pressure vanishes, so the circuit stops shrinking — S³martCirc retains a very large set of nodes while its accuracy drop stays near zero. The paper infers that baselines which optimize only task faithfulness effectively operate at this degenerate extreme, which explains their bloated circuits, and that both objective terms are necessary.

ANSWER Q16: FI is computed from the node's activations on task-specific data — i.e., from the token-geometry of the inputs it actually receives in that task. Since role assignment is a property of the node-in-context rather than an intrinsic property of the node, the same component can legitimately be functional in one task and passthrough in another.

ANSWER Q17: The answer is the automatic role-classification stage driven by the functional-information (FI) classification loss. It computes FI — a scalar measuring how much a node alters the pairwise similarity structure of its input — which makes the otherwise subjective notion of "role" a measurable, differentiable quantity that can enter the training objective.

ANSWER Q18: Although Activation Patching matches S³martCirc's IOI circuit recovery, S³martCirc achieves a substantially better (smaller/negative) accuracy drop on GPT-2 IOI, whereas Activation Patching's matched recovery comes with a larger drop — i.e., S³martCirc's circuit is more faithful at comparable recovery. (Best estimate of the Table 1 comparison; the precise numbers I don't have.)

ANSWER Q19: It would reintroduce the second stated challenge — functional roles are subjective and task-specific, requiring human judgment to define. An objective built around IOI-specific roles (S-inhibition, name mover, etc.) has no analogue in the Acronym task, so the loss would have to be redesigned and re-anchored to new human-labeled roles for every new task, destroying transferability.

ANSWER Q20: Both are classified as passthrough. A bridge head relays letter information between other components, and a name mover head copies name content to the output position; neither rewrites the similarity structure of the information it carries, so under the Figure 1 mapping both transport-only roles map to passthrough despite their different task-specific names.

ANSWER Q21: The Random baseline ends up with a much larger circuit and a far worse accuracy drop than S³martCirc (equivalently, at comparable size its faithfulness collapses). The paper's point is that a small circuit is only meaningful when it preserves behavior: S³martCirc is compact *because* it identified the right nodes, so circuit size must be interpreted jointly with the accuracy drop, not as a standalone achievement.

ANSWER Q22: Roughly an order of magnitude faster (on the order of ~10×; I don't know the exact table entry). Activation Patching is expensive because it runs clean and corrupted forward passes for each component individually across the dataset, so its cost scales linearly with the number of heads/neurons, whereas S³martCirc optimizes all node coefficients jointly in a single training run.

ANSWER Q23: P_circ is the full model with all non-circuit nodes ablated, and the accuracy drop is measured as full-model accuracy minus P_circ accuracy. Once a circuit contains all genuinely important nodes, additionally removing the remaining nodes eliminates noisy or interfering computations, so P_circ can actually outperform the full model — hence a better circuit yields a negative (improvement) drop rather than merely approaching zero, consistent with the paper's view that important nodes are those sufficient for the behavior.

ANSWER Q24: Under the negative-log confidence term, a coefficient of 0.5 incurs −ln(0.5) ≈ 0.69 nats, whereas a coefficient of 1.0 incurs 0. Because the penalty grows superlinearly as coefficients move away from 1, training is pushed toward confident, near-one-hot role assignments instead of hedged mixtures across the three coefficients.

ANSWER Q25: With α = 0 the objective reduces to the pure sparsity/minimality term, which is trivially optimized by keeping nothing. The faithfulness goal — that the circuit preserve the model's task behavior/output — would no longer be enforced at all.

ANSWER Q26: Per the appendix, the remaining Table 1 settings (the Qwen runs, and the Acronym setting) used a different α than the GPT-2 IOI optimum identified in the parameter analysis (best recollection of the setup; exact values I don't know). This implies the "best α" is model- and task-dependent, so the parameter-analysis finding is qualitative guidance rather than a universal constant.

ANSWER Q27: No. The paper's justification for labeling 10.10 differently from 8.11 rested on prior evidence that 10.10 does more than relay — i.e., it also transforms information — whereas 8.11 purely bridges. If 10.10 were shown to act only as a Bridge head under every intervention, the bridge → passthrough mapping would make S³martCirc's functional label unjustified and it would count as a disagreement.

ANSWER Q28: Because Activation Patching achieves that result at a vastly higher compute cost, equal quality from it is less impressive. The runtime appendix shows AP's wall-clock time is orders of magnitude larger, since it requires separate clean/corrupted forward passes per component over the dataset, while S³martCirc reaches the same drop in one mask-optimization run.

ANSWER Q29: FI never compares raw feature vectors; it compares the token × token pairwise-similarity (Gram) structure of input and output. The feature dimension is contracted away by the dot products, so both the d_model-dimensional input and even a 1-dimensional neuron output yield comparable N×N token-similarity matrices (via their off-diagonal entries).

ANSWER Q1: The paper concludes that continuous-mask optimization by itself is not the source of S³martCirc's advantage, since Prune. and IBCircuit share that machinery yet lag far behind. It credits the role-classification stage — the alternating training in which functional (FI-based) role information feeds back into which nodes are discovered as important.

ANSWER Q2: This would reintroduce the second challenge — functional roles are subjective and task-specific. Labels like "S-inhibition head" and "name mover head" are human-assigned categories from the hand-built IOI circuit; the Acronym task has no such categories (its heads do different jobs, e.g., letter moving), so a classification objective over IOI-specific classes would have no valid targets there and could not transfer without fresh manual analysis.

ANSWER Q3: The classification-first variant (S³martCirc-CF), which gives discovery access to role/functional information in a single pass without alternation. It outperformed the discovery-first variant (DF), showing functional information helps discovery per se, but it still trailed full S³martCirc, showing that alternation adds further gains on top.

ANSWER Q4: A node is a candidate when its combined role mass exceeds its unimportant mass (c_f + c_p > c_u, i.e., c_u is low enough). A classification-stage gradient update can raise c_f or c_p and lower c_u; if that flips the inequality, a previously excluded node becomes a candidate for the next discovery steps — so learning roles concretely changes a node's importance status, not merely the reverse.

ANSWER Q5: The classification-first variant (CF) implements the reversed ordering (roles before discovery). Yes — because CF still underperforms the full alternating method, the paper argues the gains come from treating the two stages as a single jointly (alternately) optimized problem rather than from merely reordering them.

ANSWER Q6: The paper defines roles by information transformation measured via the FI metric and assigns them by optimizing the role coefficients — a node's causal effect on the final answer is the importance (discovery) question, not the role question. A passthrough node can be causally decisive while merely relaying information, so "strongly affects the answer" does not imply "functional"; the reader is conflating importance with role.

ANSWER Q7: Best guess: roughly two orders of magnitude faster (~100×). The cost comes from Activation Patching needing a separate patched forward pass for every component (each head/neuron, per position), so its runtime scales with nodes × positions × examples, whereas S³martCirc learns all masks jointly in one training run.

ANSWER Q8: The normalization (sum-to-one) term of Eq. 5 — e.g., the (Σc − 1)²-style penalty — becomes redundant, because softmax outputs already lie on the simplex by construction. The confidence term would still be needed to push assignments toward one-hot.

ANSWER Q9: Best guess from Table 1: the Random baseline uses a much larger circuit yet still suffers a worse (less negative) accuracy drop than S³martCirc, whose circuit is far smaller with a better drop. Per the paper's reasoning, a circuit only counts as better if it is smaller at equal-or-better accuracy, so S³martCirc's compactness reflects finding the right nodes rather than merely aggressive pruning.

ANSWER Q10: FI is computed per task, from the node's activations on that task's data distribution. Because the measured input→output information preservation is task-dependent, the same node can legitimately be labeled passthrough in one task and functional in another.

ANSWER Q11: Yes, it would count as agreement. Under Figure 1's mapping, mover-type heads (Letter Movers, like Name Movers) map to the passthrough general role because they relocate token information without transforming it, so a passthrough label on 11.4 matches the human-derived circuit.

ANSWER Q12: Best guess: per the appendix, the other three Table 1 settings (GPT-2 Acronym, Qwen IOI, Qwen Acronym) used different α values than the best α identified for GPT-2 IOI. This implies the parameter-analysis optimum is specific to GPT-2 IOI — α must be retuned per model and task — so the finding's scope is limited rather than universal.

ANSWER Q13: At α = 1.0, S³martCirc's GPT-2 IOI results degrade toward the mask-only baselines (worse accuracy drop and recovery), because the discovery objective collapses to the pure task/faithfulness term with no functional guidance. The paper infers that the baselines effectively operate in exactly this regime — lacking the role/FI signal — which explains their poor performance.

ANSWER Q14: FI compares input and output through their pairwise token-similarity structure (n_tokens × n_tokens Gram/CKA-style matrices), which has the same shape regardless of the feature dimension. So even a neuron's scalar output can be compared directly with its d_model-dimensional input.

ANSWER Q15: No. The paper's justification relies on prior evidence that 10.10 does something beyond relaying (an information-transforming function), unlike 8.11; if 10.10 were purely a Bridge (relay) head under every intervention, the Figure 1 mapping would predict passthrough, and S³martCirc's differing label for 10.10 would lose its rationale.

ANSWER Q16: If both terms reward FI, then a high-FI (information-preserving) node is rewarded regardless of which label it receives, so the gradient no longer separates transformers from relayers. Role assignment would be decided only by tie-breaking/confidence terms, collapsing the intended dichotomy (functional = transforms/low FI; passthrough = preserves/high FI).

ANSWER Q17: The metric gives it FI = 1 (perfect preservation of off-diagonal similarities). The classification loss rewards c_p in proportion to FI, so with maximal FI the loss is minimized by pushing c_p → 1: the node is driven to the passthrough role, as intended for a pure relay.

ANSWER Q18: The answer is the role-classification stage built on the FI (functional information) metric. It computes a measurable, differentiable quantity — how much a node's output preserves its input's token-representation structure — allowing roles to enter and be learned within the optimization objective instead of being hand-assigned.

ANSWER Q19: P_circ keeps only the circuit (candidate) nodes and ablates all others, and the accuracy drop is measured relative to the full model. The paper's rationale is that important nodes are sufficient for the behavior while unimportant nodes mostly add noise, so a better circuit loses nothing and can even exceed full-model accuracy — hence the better the discovery, the more negative the drop.

ANSWER Q20: They should expect a worse (less negative) accuracy drop than with k = 6, and degraded IOI circuit recovery (less overlap with the known IOI heads). With too few classification steps per iteration, the role coefficients are under-trained and give poorer guidance back to discovery.

ANSWER Q21: One iteration consists of one discovery step plus k classification steps, so 10 post-warmup iterations with k = 6 give 10 discovery steps and 60 classification steps. The paper warms up first because the two stages are interdependent: role estimates are meaningless while the masks/candidate set are still near-random, so alternating from the very first step would just pass noise between the stages.

ANSWER Q22: Because an equal accuracy drop says nothing about cost: Activation Patching pays orders of magnitude more compute, requiring a separate patched forward pass per component, as the runtime appendix quantifies. S³martCirc achieves the same drop in a single mask-training run, so its result should be weighted more heavily.

ANSWER Q23: Yes — it is a candidate, because the combined role mass c_f + c_p = 0.60 exceeds c_u = 0.40. However, Eq. 1's hard assignment takes the argmax, which is c_u, so it would be labeled "unimportant" — illustrating that soft candidacy and the hard evaluation-time label can disagree.

ANSWER Q24: In DF, classification receives a fixed candidate set chosen without functional information, so any functionally important node pruned early can never be recovered. Alternating training re-opens candidacy each iteration using the latest role coefficients, so classification continually trains on an improving, functionally informed candidate set instead of being locked into the initial poor one.

ANSWER Q25: With α = 0, Eq. 2 reduces to the pure functional-guidance (role/FI-alignment) term. The goal of preserving the model's task performance (faithfulness to the original outputs) is no longer enforced, so the masks can drift to whatever satisfies the role term regardless of behavior.

ANSWER Q26: A coefficient of 1.0 incurs no confidence penalty, while 0.5 incurs the maximum per-coefficient penalty (0.25 under the c·(1−c)-style term). This gap pushes coefficients toward 0 or 1 — confident, near-one-hot role assignments — rather than hedged 50/50 splits.

ANSWER Q27: While their IOI recovery is comparable, S³martCirc's accuracy drop on GPT-2 IOI is clearly more negative than Activation Patching's — its circuit-only model stays closer to (or above) full-model accuracy, whereas AP's circuit loses more. So at similar recovery, S³martCirc is more faithful (and, per the runtime results, far cheaper).

ANSWER Q28: Yes — previous token heads receive the same general label (passthrough) in both tasks, since they copy prior-token information without transforming it. This illustrates that the dichotomy is task-general: identical functional behavior maps to the same general role even when the task and fine-grained circuit context differ.

ANSWER Q29: Both would be classified as passthrough. A bridge head and a name mover head both transport existing token information to new positions rather than transforming it (high FI), and Figure 1 maps such relay/mover roles onto the passthrough general role.

ANSWER Q1: The off-diagonal entries of Sim(Y) are −1, and FI = ||Sim(X) − Sim(Y)||_F / ||Sim(X)||_F = √(2·1.5²) / √(2·1 + 2·0.5²) = √4.5/√2.5 ≈ 1.34. The paper sets a feedforward neuron's output dimension to 1 (a scalar per token), so cosine similarity between outputs reduces to sign agreement, and opposite signs give cos = −1 (diagonals remain 1). Comparing Sim(Y) with Sim(X) is legitimate because the similarity operator maps both the input (dimension d_model) and the output (dimension 1) into the same T×T token–token similarity space, so the Frobenius comparison is well-defined despite the differing feature dimensions.

ANSWER Q2: Best guess: the paper classifies S-inhibition heads as passthrough and negative name mover heads as functional. Its dichotomy is based on what a node does to the representation — whether it preserves the input's similarity structure (relaying subject-identity information, as S-inhibition heads do) or transforms it (negative name movers write a sign-flipped version of name information, sharply changing Sim) — not on the semantic content the node handles. The critic's reasoning is therefore rejected: processing the same kind of information does not imply the same role, because roles track the operation performed, not the information type.

ANSWER Q3: Best guess: Eq. 4 updates the passthrough coefficient and the functional coefficient (the two role coefficients), and only for the candidate nodes currently selected by the preceding Important Node Discovery step; it never touches the third coefficient, the node mask/gate that discovery itself learns. Because the next discovery step runs its masked forward pass and task-loss optimization through these role coefficients (functional output vs. identity path), a node reclassified toward passthrough contributes little functional signal and its mask is pruned (while functional-boosted nodes are retained), so the set of nodes treated as the circuit changes.

ANSWER Q4: On task A, FI = 3/2 = 1.5 (> 0.5), so the classification loss pushes the node toward the functional role; on task B, FI = 3/8 = 0.375 (< 0.5), pushing it toward passthrough. This illustrates the limitation noted in the conclusion that FI is input/task-dependent: the identical node with the identical absolute representational change gets opposite roles purely because FI is normalized by ||Sim(X)||_F, which varies with the data distribution.

ANSWER Q5: The component is the similarity-operator-based Functional Importance measure (FI), the core of the Important Node Classification stage, which answers the second challenge: telling genuine computation apart from mere information relay, i.e., assigning roles rather than just importance scores. For this node, Sim(X) = [[1, 0.8],[0.8, 1]] and Sim(Y) = [[1, 0.6],[0.6, 1]], so FI = √(2·0.2²) / √(2·1 + 2·0.8²) = √0.08/√3.28 ≈ 0.156. Producing a single small value like this (well below the 0.5 decision point) quantitatively flags the node as near-passthrough — it barely alters token-token geometry — which is exactly the role discrimination that standard patching-based discovery cannot provide.

ANSWER Q6: With Eq. 4's linear dependence, the loss decreases at rate (1 − FI) = 0.75 per unit increase of the passthrough coefficient and at rate FI = 0.25 per unit increase of the functional coefficient — a factor of 3 — so the passthrough role is favored (consistent with FI = 0.25 indicating little transformation). The two rates are equal when 1 − FI = FI, i.e., at FI = 0.5.

ANSWER Q1: Eq. (4) updates the functional and passthrough coefficients of every node in the candidate circuit produced by the preceding Important Node Discovery step. It does not update the third, knockout/non-importance or discovery-membership coefficient. Because the next discovery stage recomputes membership from the updated effective gates and their effect on the task loss, shifting those two coefficients can move a node across the inclusion threshold.

ANSWER Q2: The paper classifies S-inhibition heads as functional/processing nodes and negative name mover heads as informational/passthrough nodes. Its dichotomy depends on whether a component transforms relational representations or primarily transports them, not on the semantic content involved; thus negatively moving name information remains information transport.

ANSWER Q3: At \(FI=0.25\), increasing the passthrough coefficient decreases the loss at rate \(1-FI=0.75\), while increasing the functional coefficient decreases it at rate \(FI=0.25\). The passthrough/informational role is therefore favored by a factor of \(3\), and the rates are equal at \(FI=0.5\).

ANSWER Q4: The FI values are \(3/2=1.5\) on task A and \(3/8=0.375\) on task B, pushing the node toward the functional role on A and the passthrough/informational role on B. This illustrates the paper’s stated limitation that FI is input/task- and representation-scale-dependent, so a node need not receive a stable universal role.

ANSWER Q5: Oppositely signed scalar outputs have cosine similarity \(-1\), so \(\operatorname{Sim}(Y)_{12}=\operatorname{Sim}(Y)_{21}=-1\). Thus \(FI=\frac{\sqrt{2(1.5)^2}}{\sqrt{2(1+0.5^2)}}=\frac{3}{\sqrt5}\approx1.342\). The similarity operator maps both the original \(d\)-dimensional token vectors and the neuron’s scalar outputs into the same \(2\times2\) token-token similarity space.

ANSWER Q6: The relevant component is the FI-based Important Node Classification component. Here \(FI=\frac{|0.8-0.6|}{\sqrt{1+0.8^2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{41}}\approx0.156\), indicating substantial preservation of the input token geometry and favoring an informational role. This addresses the challenge of assigning functional roles automatically and comparably across heterogeneous nodes.

Roles coming from a task-agnostic, quantitative metric on activations rather than hand-specified desiderata or ablation signs (1), importance and role being optimized jointly by alternation between stages rather than read off a single mask (2), and discovery spanning both attention heads and MLP neurons (3) are attributed to the framework under discussion (FUD; S³martCirc), which folds an abstract, quantitative notion of role directly into discovery, against the complementary line in which continuous masks over components are optimized under sparsity constraints (Frankle and Carbin 2019; Bhaskar et al. 2024), exemplified by the information bottleneck objective of the bottlenecked extractor (BE; IBCircuit) (Bian et al. 2026) and by behavior-specific mask learning (Li and Janson 2024), with component interactions captured better than by patching while most such modeling reports only which components matter, not how they contribute. Circuit extraction is formulated by BE as an optimization problem balancing behavioral fidelity with an information bottleneck objective (Bian et al. 2026), whereas masks are optimized by other approaches to isolate behavior-specific components (Li and Janson 2024). Model behavior is explained by the central explanatory program (CEP; mechanistic interpretability, MI) through identification of the components responsible for it (Bereska and Gavves 2024; Sharkey et al. 2025; Rai et al. 2024), the locus abstraction (LA; circuit) being central, and most work follows a where-then-what paradigm (Méloux et al. 2025a; García-Carrasco et al. 2024b; Chandna et al. 2025) in which components are localized via substitutionary probes (SP; patching-based interventions) (Wang et al. 2022; Meng et al. 2022; García-Carrasco et al. 2024a; Heimersheim and Nanda 2024) or first-order surrogates (FOS; gradient-based approximations) (Syed et al. 2023; Hanna et al. 2024) and their roles are then interpreted manually. Reuse of components across tasks with consistent roles (Merullo et al. 2024), localization of roles to individual neurons (Nikankin et al. 2026), and functional equivalence of structurally distinct LA (Haklay et al. 2026) indicate that functional roles are not task-specific, and the costliness of such interventions, their isolated evaluation of components, the subjectivity of the interpretation step, and the difficulty of scaling it remain attached to the manual where-then-what procedure.
